note: Dictating a clinic note on an 89-year-old female seen in the geriatrics outpatient clinic for frailty and unintentional weight loss. Her daughter brought her in today. The patient lives alone and tells me she has lost about twelve pounds over the past four months, correction, about ten pounds by the clinic scale. She reports a poor appetite and says food tastes bland. She feels weak and tired, and she has trouble climbing the stairs to her apartment. She denies nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, diarrhea, and difficulty swallowing. She denies fever and night sweats, and there is no blood in the stool. Her only chronic problem is hypertension, treated with amlodipine five mg daily, and she takes nothing else. Today her weight is ninety-eight pounds, blood pressure 124 over 70, heart rate 72, temperature 98.2. On exam she looks thin and frail, mucous membranes are moist, heart is regular, lungs are clear, and the abdomen is soft and nontender without masses. Gait is slow and she pushes up with both hands to rise from the chair. Mini-Cog score is four out of five. Impression is frailty with unintentional weight loss, most likely from reduced oral intake. Plan is to check a CBC, a comprehensive metabolic panel, a TSH, and an albumin level today. Start an oral nutritional supplement twice a day between meals. Refer to a dietitian and to physical therapy for strength training. Continue amlodipine five mg daily. Follow up in four weeks to recheck her weight.
summary: An 89-year-old female was seen in geriatrics clinic for frailty and unintentional weight loss of about ten pounds over four months, with poor appetite, weakness, fatigue, and trouble climbing stairs. She denied nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, diarrhea, difficulty swallowing, fever, night sweats, and blood in the stool. Her only chronic condition is hypertension, treated with amlodipine 5 mg daily. She looked thin and frail with a slow gait, and her weight was 98 pounds. The impression was frailty with unintentional weight loss, most likely from reduced oral intake, and labs, a nutritional supplement, dietitian and physical therapy referrals, and a four-week follow-up were planned.

soap.subjective: 89-year-old female with frailty and unintentional weight loss of about ten pounds over four months (corrected from twelve by the clinic scale). Reports poor appetite, bland-tasting food, weakness, fatigue, and trouble climbing the stairs to her apartment. Denies nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, diarrhea, difficulty swallowing, fever, night sweats, and blood in the stool. Lives alone; her daughter brought her in. PMH hypertension on amlodipine 5 mg daily; takes no other medications.
soap.objective: Weight 98 pounds, blood pressure 124/70, heart rate 72, temperature 98.2. Thin and frail appearing, moist mucous membranes, regular heart, clear lungs, soft nontender abdomen without masses. Slow gait; uses both hands to rise from the chair. Mini-Cog score 4 out of 5.
soap.assessment: Frailty with unintentional weight loss, most likely from reduced oral intake. Hypertension.
plan: CBC, comprehensive metabolic panel, TSH, and albumin level today
Start an oral nutritional supplement twice a day between meals
Refer to a dietitian and to physical therapy for strength training
Continue amlodipine 5 mg daily
Follow up in four weeks to recheck weight

note:
60-year-old female, joint ENT/ophtho clinic, c/o sinus trouble x 6 mo. Limited health literacy: used plain language and teach-back, pt brought a bag of bottles, unsure of drug names.
CC: stuffy nose, face pressure, thick yellow-green drainage, PND
Reduced smell x 4 mo
Night cough from PND
Both eyes watery + "pressure behind my eyes" L>R x 2 mo
Denies fever, chills, vision loss, double vision, pain w/ eye movement, eyelid swelling, nosebleeds
No facial numbness, no HA, no eye discharge
Tx so far: finished Augmentin 875/125 BID x 10 d about 3 wk ago, little help. Using OTC oxymetazoline "the nose spray" 2-3x/day x 3 mo, congested again as soon as it wears off.
PMH: HTN, T2DM, asthma, GERD. No prior sinus surgery.
Social: never smoker, no alcohol, lives w/ husband. No recent dental pain.
NKDA
Meds (read from bottles):
 lisinopril 20 mg daily
 metformin - pt states 500 mg BID, bottle says 1000 mg BID, correction: takes 1000 mg BID
 albuterol HFA PRN
 fluticasone nasal spray 1 spray each nostril daily
 omeprazole 20 mg daily
 oxymetazoline OTC
Vitals: BP 148/86, HR 78, RR 16, SpO2 97% RA, Temp 98.4 F
Exam: NAD. Face mildly TTP over maxillary sinuses bilat. Anterior rhinoscopy: edematous turbinates, thick mucus.
Nasal endoscopy: mucopurulent drainage R middle meatus, edematous mucosa, no polyps, septum midline, no mass.
Eyes: VA 20/30 OU, PERRL, EOMI w/o pain, no proptosis, no lid edema, conjunctivae mildly injected OU w/ watery discharge. IOP 16 OU. Dilated fundus exam: no diabetic retinopathy OU.
Data: CT sinuses from PCP 2 mo ago, per report bilat maxillary + ethmoid mucosal thickening, R maxillary air-fluid level, no orbital extension. Labs today: Cr 0.9, eGFR 84, A1c 7.9%.
Imp: chronic rhinosinusitis w/o polyps, failed 1 course of Augmentin. Rhinitis medicamentosa from oxymetazoline overuse. No orbital involvement. Watery eyes likely from nasal obstruction, r/o allergic conjunctivitis. HTN above goal today, f/u w/ PCP. T2DM A1c 7.9%.
Rec:
 STOP oxymetazoline now (rebound congestion), explained w/ picture handout
 fluticasone increase to 2 sprays each nostril daily
 start saline rinses daily w/ distilled water
 start doxycycline 100 mg BID x 21 d w/ food + full glass of water, sun protection
 culture R middle meatus sent, adjust abx per result
 artificial tears PRN both eyes up to QID
 cont lisinopril, metformin 1000 mg BID, albuterol PRN, omeprazole
 repeat CT sinuses if no better at f/u
 diabetic eye exam done today, next in 1 yr
 teach-back: pt repeated "stop the clear spray, blue spray 2 puffs each side every morning, rinse my nose daily, new pill twice a day with food." Pill card w/ pictures given.
 pt asked if the sinus pressure can hurt her eyes: reassured, no orbital involvement on exam today
 f/u 3 wk. ER if eyelid swelling, vision change or double vision, high fever, severe HA
summary: A 60-year-old female with limited health literacy was seen in a joint ENT and ophthalmology clinic for six months of sinus symptoms and two months of watery eyes. She had failed one course of Augmentin and had been overusing oxymetazoline. Endoscopy showed mucopurulent drainage in the right middle meatus without polyps, and the eye exam showed no orbital involvement or diabetic retinopathy. The impression was chronic rhinosinusitis with rhinitis medicamentosa. Oxymetazoline was stopped, fluticasone increased, doxycycline started with a culture sent, and follow-up planned in three weeks with teach-back instructions.

soap.subjective: 60-year-old female with limited health literacy (teach-back used; brought bottles, unsure of drug names) with 6 months of stuffy nose, face pressure, thick yellow-green drainage, postnasal drip, reduced smell, and night cough, plus 2 months of watery eyes with pressure behind the eyes, left greater than right. Denies fever, chills, vision loss, double vision, pain with eye movement, eyelid swelling, nosebleeds, facial numbness, headache, and eye discharge. Finished Augmentin 875/125 BID for 10 days about 3 weeks ago with little help, and has used OTC oxymetazoline 2-3 times a day for 3 months. PMH HTN, T2DM, asthma, GERD. NKDA. Home medications: lisinopril 20 mg daily, metformin 1000 mg BID (patient first said 500 mg, corrected from the bottle), albuterol HFA PRN, fluticasone nasal spray 1 spray each nostril daily, omeprazole 20 mg daily.
soap.objective: BP 148/86, HR 78, RR 16, SpO2 97% RA, Temp 98.4 F. NAD; mild maxillary sinus tenderness bilaterally; edematous turbinates with thick mucus. Nasal endoscopy: mucopurulent drainage in the right middle meatus, edematous mucosa, no polyps, midline septum, no mass. Eyes: VA 20/30 OU, PERRL, EOMI without pain, no proptosis, no lid edema, conjunctivae mildly injected OU with watery discharge, IOP 16 OU, dilated fundus exam without diabetic retinopathy. CT sinuses from PCP 2 months ago per report: bilateral maxillary and ethmoid mucosal thickening, right maxillary air-fluid level, no orbital extension. Labs: Cr 0.9, eGFR 84, A1c 7.9%.
soap.assessment: Chronic rhinosinusitis without polyps that failed one course of Augmentin; rhinitis medicamentosa from oxymetazoline overuse; no orbital involvement; watery eyes likely from nasal obstruction, rule out allergic conjunctivitis; HTN above goal today; T2DM with A1c 7.9%.
plan: Stop oxymetazoline now because of rebound congestion; explained with a picture handout
Increase fluticasone to 2 sprays each nostril daily
Start daily saline rinses with distilled water
Start doxycycline 100 mg BID for 21 days with food and a full glass of water; sun protection
Send culture of the right middle meatus and adjust antibiotics per result
Artificial tears PRN both eyes up to QID
Continue lisinopril, metformin 1000 mg BID, albuterol PRN, and omeprazole
Repeat CT sinuses if no improvement at follow-up
Diabetic eye exam done today; next in 1 year
Teach-back completed and pill card with pictures given
Follow up in 3 weeks; ER for eyelid swelling, vision change or double vision, high fever, or severe headache

note:
52-year-old male, kidney transplant f/u, HD#3 (readmitted 3 d ago).
Hx: DDKT 3 yr ago for ESRD from IgA nephropathy, baseline Cr 1.4. HTN.
Recent admit for CAP, d/c'd 10 d ago on clarithromycin 500 mg BID x 7 d (finished 3 d ago). Tacrolimus (tac) dose was not adjusted.
Readmitted c/o hand tremor, nausea, HA x 4 d. Tac trough on admit 17.8 ng/mL (goal 5-8). Cr 2.3 on admit.
Overnight: no events. Tremor improved, nausea better, tolerating diet.
Denies fever, cough, dysuria, diarrhea, decreased urine output, graft pain
Meds:
 tacrolimus held x 2 doses, now 3 mg BID (was 4 mg BID)
 mycophenolate 500 mg BID
 prednisone 5 mg daily
 amlodipine 5 mg daily
 IV NS 75 mL/h
Vitals: BP 142/88, HR 80, RR 16, Temp 98.1 F, SpO2 98% RA
Exam: NAD, fine tremor both hands, RRR, lungs CTAB, abd soft NT, graft site RLQ nontender, no edema
Labs today: Cr 1.8 (2.3 on admit), BUN 31, K 4.9, Na 138, Hgb 11.6, WBC 7.2. Tac trough this AM 9.4.
UA: no blood, trace protein. Renal US w/ doppler: no hydronephrosis, RI 0.68, normal graft perfusion.
Impression: AKI on transplanted kidney from supratherapeutic tacrolimus level due to clarithromycin interaction, improving. Tremor resolving. BP mildly elevated.
Recs:
 cont tacrolimus 3 mg BID, tac trough q AM x 3 d, goal 5-8
 cont mycophenolate 500 mg BID and prednisone 5 mg daily
 cont IV NS 75 mL/h until PO intake solid, then stop
 avoid macrolides, azoles and other CYP3A4 inhibitors, chart alert added
 cont amlodipine 5 mg daily, recheck BP
 BMP daily
 anticipate d/c in 1-2 d if Cr < 1.6, transplant clinic f/u 1 wk w/ tac trough
summary: A 52-year-old male with a kidney transplant from three years ago and a recent admission for pneumonia was readmitted with tremor, nausea, headache, and a creatinine of 2.3. His tacrolimus trough was 17.8 ng/mL after a clarithromycin course. He denied fever, cough, dysuria, diarrhea, decreased urine output, and graft pain. The impression was acute kidney injury from a supratherapeutic tacrolimus level due to the clarithromycin interaction, improving with creatinine 1.8 and trough 9.4. Tacrolimus was reduced to 3 mg BID, IV fluids and other immunosuppression continued, macrolides and CYP3A4 inhibitors are to be avoided, and discharge is expected in 1-2 days.

soap.subjective: 52-year-old male, 3 years after a deceased-donor kidney transplant for ESRD from IgA nephropathy (baseline Cr 1.4) with HTN, readmitted 3 days ago with hand tremor, nausea, and headache for 4 days. He was discharged 10 days ago after a CAP admission on clarithromycin 500 mg BID for 7 days, and his tacrolimus was not adjusted. Admission tacrolimus trough was 17.8 ng/mL and Cr 2.3. Overnight no events; tremor and nausea are better and he is tolerating diet. Denies fever, cough, dysuria, diarrhea, decreased urine output, and graft pain.
soap.objective: BP 142/88, HR 80, RR 16, Temp 98.1 F, SpO2 98% RA. NAD, fine tremor of both hands, RRR, lungs clear, abdomen soft and nontender, graft site RLQ nontender, no edema. Labs: Cr 1.8 (2.3 on admission), BUN 31, K 4.9, Na 138, Hgb 11.6, WBC 7.2, tacrolimus trough this morning 9.4. UA with no blood and trace protein. Renal ultrasound with Doppler: no hydronephrosis, RI 0.68, normal graft perfusion.
soap.assessment: AKI on a transplanted kidney from a supratherapeutic tacrolimus level due to clarithromycin interaction, improving. Tremor resolving. BP mildly elevated.
plan: Continue tacrolimus 3 mg BID (reduced from 4 mg BID) with tacrolimus trough every AM for 3 days, goal 5-8
Continue mycophenolate 500 mg BID and prednisone 5 mg daily
Continue IV NS 75 mL/h until PO intake is solid, then stop
Avoid macrolides, azoles, and other CYP3A4 inhibitors; chart alert added
Continue amlodipine 5 mg daily and recheck BP
BMP daily
Anticipate discharge in 1-2 days if Cr is below 1.6; transplant clinic follow-up in 1 week with tacrolimus trough

note:
73-year-old male, pulm f/u for PE on anticoagulation, HD#4.
Admitted 3 d ago c/o SOB + R-sided pleuritic CP. s/p R TKA 3 wk ago.
CTPA on admit: segmental PE R lower lobe, no RV strain.
Today: SOB much better, CP improved but still pain w/ deep inspiration.
Denies hemoptysis, leg swelling, dizziness, palpitations. No bleeding (gums, urine, stool).
Meds: apixaban 10 mg BID (day 4 of 7), acetaminophen 650 mg q6h PRN for pleuritic CP
Vitals: BP 128/76, HR 82, RR 16, SpO2 96% RA, Temp 98.2 F
Exam: NAD, lungs CTAB, RRR, no JVD, calves soft + nontender, no edema, R knee incision c/d/i
Labs: Hgb 13.1, Plt 238, Cr 0.9
Impression: provoked segmental PE after recent knee surgery, clinically improving on apixaban
Rec:
 cont apixaban 10 mg BID to finish 7 d, then 5 mg BID, total 3 mo
 TTE to reassess RV
 ambulate w/ PT, check SpO2 w/ walking
 d/c home tomorrow if SpO2 > 92% w/ ambulation
 pulm clinic f/u in 3 mo, return if worse SOB, CP, or bleeding
summary: A 73-year-old male on hospital day 4 was seen by pulmonology for follow-up of a pulmonary embolism three weeks after right knee replacement. CT pulmonary angiography showed a right lower lobe segmental PE without right ventricular strain, and his dyspnea and chest pain are improving on apixaban. He denied hemoptysis, leg swelling, dizziness, palpitations, and bleeding. Vitals and exam were reassuring. The impression was a provoked segmental PE, improving, and the plan is to complete apixaban 10 mg BID for 7 days then 5 mg BID for 3 months, obtain a TTE, ambulate with PT, and discharge tomorrow if SpO2 stays above 92% with walking.

soap.subjective: 73-year-old male on hospital day 4 for a pulmonary embolism, admitted 3 days ago with SOB and right-sided pleuritic chest pain, status post right TKA 3 weeks ago. CTPA showed a segmental PE in the right lower lobe with no RV strain. Today SOB is much better and chest pain is improved with some pain on deep inspiration. Denies hemoptysis, leg swelling, dizziness, palpitations, and bleeding from gums, urine, or stool. Taking apixaban 10 mg BID (day 4 of 7) and acetaminophen 650 mg q6h PRN.
soap.objective: BP 128/76, HR 82, RR 16, SpO2 96% RA, Temp 98.2 F. NAD, lungs clear bilaterally, regular rhythm, no JVD, calves soft and nontender, no edema, right knee incision clean, dry, and intact. Labs: Hgb 13.1, Plt 238, Cr 0.9.
soap.assessment: Provoked segmental PE after recent knee surgery, clinically improving on apixaban.
plan: Continue apixaban 10 mg BID to finish 7 days, then 5 mg BID for a total of 3 months
TTE to reassess the right ventricle
Ambulate with PT and check SpO2 with walking
Discharge home tomorrow if SpO2 stays above 92% with ambulation
Pulmonary clinic follow-up in 3 months; return for worse SOB, chest pain, or bleeding

note:
Doctor: Good afternoon. I see you are a 65-year-old female here at urgent care today because you want to be evaluated for ADHD. I am using a professional interpreter, so I will speak in short sentences and pause so everything gets translated. Is that okay?
Patient: Yes, that is fine. Thank you.
Doctor: Tell me what has been going on.
Patient: Since I was a girl I cannot focus. My mind wanders in conversations, I lose my keys and my glasses almost every day, and I leave projects half finished. When I came home from the hospital three weeks ago I saw how bad it is, because I forgot my pills many times.
Doctor: What were you in the hospital for?
Patient: My blood pressure was very high, 220 over something, and I had a terrible headache. They kept me four days.
Doctor: Did they scan your head?
Patient: Yes, a CT scan. They said it was normal.
Doctor: Good. Do you have trouble sitting still?
Patient: Inside I feel restless, but I can sit. I talk a lot and interrupt people, my daughter says.
Doctor: Did these problems start in school?
Patient: Yes. My teachers wrote that I daydream, and I could not finish tests on time.
Doctor: Have you felt sad or hopeless, or lost interest in things?
Patient: No, I am not depressed. I worry a little about money, but I am not sad.
Doctor: Any thoughts of harming yourself?
Patient: No, never.
Doctor: Any chest pain or palpitations?
Patient: No chest pain, no palpitations.
Doctor: Do you drink alcohol or use any drugs?
Patient: No alcohol, no drugs.
Doctor: How is your sleep?
Patient: About six hours. My husband says I snore a little.
Doctor: What medical conditions do you have?
Patient: I have diabetes, high blood pressure, an underactive thyroid, and high cholesterol.
Doctor: Let us go through your medicines. What did the hospital change?
Patient: They stopped the naproxen I took for my knees. They raised the amlodipine from 5 to 10 milligrams once a day. I also take lisinopril 20 milligrams every morning, metformin 500 milligrams twice a day, the thyroid pill levothyroxine 100 micrograms... wait, let me look at my list. The thyroid pill is 75 micrograms. And atorvastatin 40 milligrams at night.
Doctor: Okay, so levothyroxine 75 micrograms daily, not 100. Thank you for checking.
Patient: Yes, 75.
Doctor: Your hospital papers show a TSH of 2.1, an A1c of 7.2, creatinine 1.0, and an EKG with normal sinus rhythm. Today your blood pressure is 152 over 90 and your heart rate is 84. The ASRS screener you filled out in the waiting room was positive, five of six items.
Patient: What does that mean?
Doctor: It means your symptoms fit ADHD, but a screener cannot confirm it. On exam you are alert and pleasant, you asked me to repeat a few things, your speech is normal, there is no tremor, your heart is regular and your lungs are clear.
Doctor: My impression is long-standing inattention since childhood, which could be inattentive ADHD, but we cannot confirm that today. Your blood pressure is above goal, and stimulant medicines can raise blood pressure and heart rate, so I will not start one today. I will refer you to outpatient psychiatry for a full ADHD evaluation with cognitive testing. Please keep avoiding naproxen, check your blood pressure at home every morning, use a weekly pill organizer with phone alarms, and see your primary care doctor within one week about your blood pressure. Return here or go to the emergency room for a severe headache, chest pain, or confusion.
Patient: Yes, I understand. Thank you.
summary: A 65-year-old female seen at urgent care with a professional interpreter requested evaluation for ADHD, reporting lifelong inattention and forgetfulness that became evident after a hospital stay three weeks ago for severe hypertension. She denied depression, thoughts of self-harm, chest pain, palpitations, alcohol, and drugs, and had a positive ASRS screener with blood pressure 152/90. Hospital changes included stopping naproxen and raising amlodipine to 10 mg, and levothyroxine was clarified as 75 micrograms. The impression was long-standing inattention that could be inattentive ADHD, and no stimulant was started because of her blood pressure. She was referred to outpatient psychiatry for a full evaluation with cognitive testing and advised to monitor blood pressure and see primary care within one week.

soap.subjective: 65-year-old female seen with a professional interpreter, requesting ADHD evaluation. Since childhood she cannot focus, her mind wanders, she loses keys and glasses daily, leaves projects unfinished, daydreamed in school, feels restless inside, talks a lot, and interrupts people. Three weeks ago she was hospitalized for 4 days for very high blood pressure with a terrible headache and had a normal head CT; afterward she noticed she forgot her pills many times. Denies depressed mood, sadness, thoughts of harming herself, chest pain, palpitations, alcohol, and drugs; sleeps about six hours and snores a little. Has diabetes, high blood pressure, an underactive thyroid, and high cholesterol. Hospital stopped naproxen and raised amlodipine from 5 to 10 mg once a day; takes lisinopril 20 mg every morning, metformin 500 mg twice a day, levothyroxine 75 micrograms daily (she first said 100, then corrected to 75 from her list), and atorvastatin 40 mg at night.
soap.objective: Hospital results: TSH 2.1, A1c 7.2, creatinine 1.0, EKG with normal sinus rhythm, head CT normal. Today blood pressure 152/90, heart rate 84. ASRS screener positive, 5 of 6 items. Alert and pleasant, asked for a few things to be repeated, normal speech, no tremor, regular heart, clear lungs.
soap.assessment: Long-standing inattention since childhood, possible inattentive ADHD that cannot be confirmed today. Blood pressure above goal.
plan: No stimulant medicine today because stimulants can raise blood pressure and heart rate
Refer to outpatient psychiatry for a full ADHD evaluation with cognitive testing
Continue to avoid naproxen
Check blood pressure at home every morning
Use a weekly pill organizer with phone alarms
See primary care within one week about blood pressure
Return or go to the emergency room for severe headache, chest pain, or confusion

note:
Doctor: Hello, I am the emergency physician. I understand you are an 84-year-old female with a sudden, severe headache. Who is with you today?
Family member: I am her daughter and her caregiver. I live with her and help with her pills.
Doctor: Tell me what happened.
Patient: I was making tea this morning and, boom, the worst headache of my life, at the back of my head. It came on in a second.
Doctor: When was that?
Patient: About three hours ago. Then I felt sick to my stomach and I threw up once.
Doctor: Any weakness, numbness, trouble speaking, or vision changes?
Patient: No weakness, no numbness, my speech is fine, and my vision is fine.
Doctor: Neck pain or fever?
Patient: My neck is a little sore, but it is not stiff. No fever.
Doctor: Any falls or bumps on your head?
Patient: No, I have not fallen.
Family member: Mom, you did fall. Last week in the kitchen you hit the left side of your head on the cabinet door. You said it was nothing.
Patient: Oh, I forgot about that. Yes, I did.
Doctor: Thank you for telling me. Any chest pain or trouble breathing?
Patient: No chest pain, no trouble breathing.
Doctor: What medical conditions does she have?
Family member: High blood pressure, atrial fibrillation, type 2 diabetes, kidney disease stage 3, and high cholesterol.
Doctor: And her medicines? Is she on a blood thinner?
Family member: Yes, apixaban 5 mg twice a day. Sorry, let me read the bottle. It says 2.5 mg twice a day, the dose was lowered. She also takes amlodipine 10 mg daily, metoprolol succinate 50 mg daily, atorvastatin 40 mg at night, and metformin 500 mg twice a day. The metoprolol was increased from 25 to 50 mg two weeks ago by her primary care doctor.
Doctor: When was the last apixaban dose?
Family member: This morning around seven.
Doctor: Any allergies to medicines?
Family member: No known allergies.
Doctor: Her vitals are blood pressure 188/96, heart rate 78 and irregular, respiratory rate 18, oxygen saturation 97% on room air, and temperature 98.0. On exam she is awake and alert with a GCS of 15. Pupils are equal and reactive, her face is symmetric, speech is clear, strength is normal in all four limbs, and there is no drift. Her neck is supple with mild muscle tenderness but no meningismus. There is a small bruise over the left temple. Labs show hemoglobin 11.8, platelets 190, creatinine 1.6, sodium 138, potassium 4.2, and glucose 142. The CT head without contrast shows an acute subdural hematoma on the left, about 8 mm thick, with no midline shift and no subarachnoid blood.
Family member: Oh no. Is that from the fall?
Doctor: That is the most likely cause, and the apixaban makes bleeding worse. My impression is an acute subdural hematoma in a patient on a blood thinner. We will stop the apixaban and reverse it with 4-factor prothrombin complex concentrate. I will give labetalol 10 mg IV to bring her systolic blood pressure under 160, start levetiracetam 500 mg twice a day to prevent seizures, and give acetaminophen 650 mg for the headache. No ibuprofen or aspirin. I will also hold the metformin. Neurosurgery is being consulted, she will be admitted to the neuro ICU, and we will repeat the CT head in six hours.
Patient: Will I need surgery?
Doctor: Neurosurgery will decide after the repeat scan. We will watch you very closely tonight.
Family member: Okay, we understand. Thank you.
summary: An 84-year-old female with a sudden severe headache was brought to the emergency department with her daughter, who revealed a fall with a head strike last week. She takes apixaban, which the daughter corrected from 5 mg to 2.5 mg twice a day after reading the bottle. Blood pressure was 188/96, the neurologic exam was nonfocal, and CT head showed an acute left subdural hematoma about 8 mm thick without midline shift. The apixaban was stopped and reversed with prothrombin complex concentrate, and labetalol, levetiracetam, and acetaminophen were given, with metformin held. Neurosurgery was consulted, she will be admitted to the neuro ICU, and the CT head will be repeated in six hours.

soap.subjective: 84-year-old female with sudden severe headache at the back of the head about three hours ago, the worst of her life, followed by nausea and one episode of vomiting. Denies weakness, numbness, fever, chest pain, and trouble breathing; neck is a little sore but not stiff. Initially denied falls, but her daughter and caregiver reported a fall last week with a blow to the left side of her head. History of high blood pressure, atrial fibrillation, type 2 diabetes, kidney disease stage 3, and high cholesterol. Medications: apixaban 2.5 mg twice a day (daughter first said 5 mg, corrected from the bottle; last dose this morning), amlodipine 10 mg daily, metoprolol succinate 50 mg daily (increased from 25 mg two weeks ago), atorvastatin 40 mg at night, and metformin 500 mg twice a day. No known allergies.
soap.objective: Blood pressure 188/96, heart rate 78 and irregular, respiratory rate 18, oxygen saturation 97% on room air, temperature 98.0. Awake and alert, GCS 15, pupils equal and reactive, symmetric face, clear speech, normal strength in all four limbs, no drift, supple neck with mild muscle tenderness and no meningismus, small bruise over the left temple. Labs: hemoglobin 11.8, platelets 190, creatinine 1.6, sodium 138, potassium 4.2, glucose 142. CT head without contrast: acute left subdural hematoma about 8 mm thick, no midline shift, no subarachnoid blood.
soap.assessment: Acute subdural hematoma, most likely from last week's fall, in a patient on apixaban.
plan: Stop apixaban and reverse with 4-factor prothrombin complex concentrate
Labetalol 10 mg IV to bring systolic blood pressure under 160
Start levetiracetam 500 mg twice a day for seizure prevention
Acetaminophen 650 mg for headache; no ibuprofen or aspirin
Hold metformin
Neurosurgery consultation and admission to the neuro ICU
Repeat CT head in six hours

note:
Hospital day 3 for an 80-year-old female admitted with melena and symptomatic anemia, found to have an upper gastrointestinal bleed from a gastric ulcer. She had been taking over-the-counter naproxen several times a week for knee osteoarthritis, which is the likely cause. EGD yesterday showed a 1.5 cm gastric ulcer with a clean base and no active bleeding, and biopsies for H. pylori were taken. There were no events overnight. Since the endoscopy she has had no further melena, no hematemesis, no abdominal pain, and no lightheadedness, and she ate breakfast without nausea. She also denies chest pain and shortness of breath.

Current medications include pantoprazole 40 mg IV twice daily, which we are converting to oral pantoprazole 40 mg twice daily today, and acetaminophen 650 mg every 6 hours as needed for knee pain. Her home lisinopril 10 mg daily for hypertension was held on admission and remains on hold. Naproxen has been discontinued permanently.

On exam this morning she is comfortable, with mild conjunctival pallor, a soft, nontender, nondistended abdomen, and no leg edema. Vitals are BP 118/64, HR 84, RR 16, Temp 98.3 F, and SpO2 96% on room air. Hemoglobin is 8.2 this morning after one unit of packed red blood cells yesterday, up from 6.9 on admission. BUN is 24, down from 41, creatinine is 0.9, and INR is 1.0.

She has an upper gastrointestinal bleed from an NSAID-associated gastric ulcer with acute blood loss anemia, both improving, plus hypertension with blood pressure currently acceptable off lisinopril. We will switch to oral pantoprazole today and advance her to a regular diet. We will recheck a CBC this afternoon and tomorrow morning and transfuse for hemoglobin below 7. Lisinopril stays on hold until her blood pressure rises and she has been eating well. We will follow the H. pylori biopsy results and treat if positive. She should avoid all NSAIDs and use acetaminophen for knee pain. If hemoglobin is stable, she can go home in one to two days on pantoprazole twice daily for 8 weeks with GI follow-up and a repeat EGD in 8 to 12 weeks to confirm healing.
summary: An 80-year-old female on hospital day 3 has an upper gastrointestinal bleed from a gastric ulcer attributed to over-the-counter naproxen for knee osteoarthritis. The plan is oral pantoprazole twice daily, a diet advance, serial CBCs, lisinopril on hold, no NSAIDs, H. pylori biopsy follow-up, and discharge in one to two days if stable.

note:
Visit modality: synchronous video visit on the patient's smartphone. The patient was at home, identity was confirmed verbally, and she consented to telehealth.

Reason for visit: infectious disease follow-up to start treatment for latent tuberculosis infection (LTBI).

History: The patient is a 70-year-old female who works rotating night and day shifts at a warehouse, so her sleep and meal times change from week to week. A workplace screening interferon-gamma release assay (IGRA) was positive 2 weeks ago. Her chest x-ray was normal, with no infiltrates or cavitation. She reports no cough, no fever, no night sweats, no weight loss, and no hemoptysis. She has no known TB contacts. She reports trouble sleeping whenever her shifts change. She has hypertension treated with lisinopril 10 mg daily. She has no history of liver disease and does not drink alcohol. Baseline AST was 24 and ALT was 19 last week.

Home measurements reported by the patient: blood pressure 132/78, pulse 70, temperature 98.2 F.

Video observation: She appears comfortable, speaks in full sentences, did not cough during the visit, and has no visible jaundice or scleral icterus. She is alert and oriented.

Impression: Latent tuberculosis infection with no symptoms or imaging findings of active TB. Hypertension stable on current therapy. Sleep disruption related to shift work.

Treatment: Start rifampin 600 mg once daily for 4 months. I chose rifampin over isoniazid because the course is shorter and a single daily dose can be tied to the time she wakes up, whatever shift she is on. She should take it on an empty stomach, an hour before or two hours after food. I counseled her that rifampin turns urine, sweat, and tears orange, that it can stain soft contact lenses, and that she should call us right away and hold the dose for nausea, vomiting, dark urine, yellow skin or eyes, or right upper abdominal pain. Rifampin does not interact with lisinopril, but she should check with us or her pharmacist before starting any new medicine. For adherence she will set two phone alarms labeled for day and night shifts, use a weekly pill organizer, and have the pharmacy mail a 30-day supply. Repeat AST and ALT before her next visit. Continue lisinopril 10 mg daily. Telehealth follow-up in 4 weeks, then monthly. She repeated the plan back accurately.

She reported no cough, fever, night sweats, weight loss, or hemoptysis and has hypertension on lisinopril, with normal baseline AST and ALT. The impression was latent tuberculosis infection without evidence of active TB. Rifampin 600 mg once daily for 4 months was started, timed to her waking hour regardless of shift, with counseling, phone alarms, a pill organizer, mailed refills, and repeat AST and ALT. Telehealth follow-up is planned in 4 weeks.

note:
Doctor: Hi there. I see you are a 28-year-old female and you are here about trouble sleeping. Tell me about it.
Patient: I have had trouble falling asleep for about eight months now. I lie there for two hours, sometimes more, and then I wake up around four and can't go back to sleep.
Doctor: How many nights a week does that happen?
Patient: Almost every night, maybe six out of seven. I am exhausted at work and my head feels foggy.
Doctor: What have you tried so far?
Patient: I take diphenhydramine, the over-the-counter sleep aid, 50 mg every night. It worked at first, but now I wake up groggy. I also take melatonin 5 mg at bedtime, and that does not do much.
Doctor: How much caffeine do you have?
Patient: Three cups of coffee a day, and the last one is around four in the afternoon. I also scroll on my phone in bed.
Doctor: Any loud snoring or waking up gasping?
Patient: No snoring, no gasping.
Doctor: Any restless legs at night?
Patient: No.
Doctor: How is your mood? Do you feel down or anxious?
Patient: A bit anxious about work, but I am not depressed.
Doctor: Any thoughts of hurting yourself?
Patient: No.
Doctor: Any chest pain or palpitations? How much alcohol do you drink?
Patient: No chest pain, no palpitations. Maybe one glass of wine on weekends.
Doctor: Do you have any other medical conditions or take any other medicines?
Patient: No. My primary care doctor checked my thyroid last month and it was normal, TSH 1.8.
Doctor: Good. Your vitals today are blood pressure 112/70, heart rate 76, and temperature 98.4. On exam your heart is regular, your lungs are clear, and there is no tremor. Your anxiety questionnaire, the GAD-7, came out at 7, which is mild.
Doctor: So this looks like chronic insomnia, with some mild anxiety and a lot of caffeine late in the day. I think the diphenhydramine is making you groggy and it stops working over time, so I want you to stop it tonight. You can continue the melatonin 5 mg at bedtime. Cut off caffeine after noon, keep the same wake time every day, keep your phone out of bed, and get up and do something quiet if you are awake for more than twenty minutes. I am also referring you to a cognitive behavioral therapy program for insomnia, which works better than sleeping pills. Follow up with your primary care doctor in four weeks, and come back sooner if your mood drops or you have any thoughts of hurting yourself.
Patient: Okay, that makes sense. Thank you.
summary: A 28-year-old female presented to urgent care with eight months of trouble falling asleep and early waking, exhaustion, and brain fog, taking nightly diphenhydramine and melatonin and drinking three coffees a day. She denied snoring, gasping, restless legs, depression, thoughts of self-harm, chest pain, and palpitations. Vitals and exam were normal, her recent TSH was 1.8, and her GAD-7 was 7. The impression was chronic insomnia with mild anxiety and late caffeine use. Diphenhydramine was stopped, melatonin continued, sleep habit changes and a cognitive behavioral therapy referral were given, and primary care follow-up is in four weeks.

note:
Doctor: Good morning. I see you are a 68-year-old male and you are here because of a fever after your trip. Tell me what happened.
Patient: I got back from India nine days ago after visiting my brother. Five days ago the fever started, with a terrible headache, aching all over, and pain behind my eyes. Two days ago I got a rash on my chest and arms.
Doctor: How high has the fever been?
Patient: 101 to 102 at home.
Doctor: Any chills or drenching sweats?
Patient: Chills, yes. No drenching sweats.
Doctor: Any vomiting, diarrhea, or belly pain?
Patient: No vomiting, no diarrhea, no belly pain. I just feel a little nauseous.
Doctor: Any cough or shortness of breath?
Patient: No cough and no shortness of breath.
Doctor: Any bleeding from your gums or nose, or blood in your stool or urine?
Patient: No bleeding at all.
Doctor: Did you get mosquito bites, and did you take malaria pills?
Patient: I got a lot of bites. I did not take any malaria pills.
Doctor: What medicines are you taking now?
Patient: Amlodipine 5 mg every morning for my blood pressure, and ibuprofen 400 mg every six hours for the fever and aches.
Doctor: And what do you do for work?
Patient: I work nights as a security guard, ten at night to six in the morning, but my days off change every week. I sleep in the daytime, so it is hard for me to come in.
Doctor: Understood, we will plan around your schedule. Your vitals today are temperature 100.8, blood pressure 118/72, heart rate 92, and oxygen saturation 98% on room air. On exam you look tired but not toxic. You have a faint flat rash on your trunk and arms, but no petechiae. Your mouth is moist, your heart is regular, your lungs are clear, your belly is soft and not tender, and there is no neck stiffness.
Doctor: Your labs from this morning show a white count of 3.1, platelets 98, hemoglobin 14.5, AST 62, and ALT 48. The malaria smears and the rapid malaria test were negative, and the dengue NS1 antigen was positive.
Patient: So I have dengue?
Doctor: Yes, my impression is dengue fever. There is no specific antiviral, so treatment is supportive. I want you to stop the ibuprofen, because it can increase bleeding risk when platelets are low. Use acetaminophen 650 mg every six hours as needed for fever, no more than 3,000 mg in a day, and drink plenty of fluids. Continue the amlodipine. Go to the emergency room right away if you have bleeding, severe belly pain, repeated vomiting, drowsiness, cold clammy skin, or trouble breathing. I will repeat a CBC in 48 hours. Since you work nights, the lab opens at seven in the morning, so come right after your shift, and I will call you with the result. Use mosquito repellent at home so you do not pass it on through bites.
Patient: Okay, I understand.
summary: A 68-year-old male night-shift worker with an irregular schedule was seen in infectious disease clinic for fever, headache, myalgias, retro-orbital pain, and a rash that began five days after returning from India. He denied vomiting, diarrhea, belly pain, cough, shortness of breath, and bleeding. He was febrile at 100.8 with a faint rash, platelets of 98, a white count of 3.1, mildly elevated AST and ALT, negative malaria testing, and a positive dengue NS1 antigen. The impression was dengue fever, and ibuprofen was stopped in favor of acetaminophen, with fluids, amlodipine continued, warning signs reviewed, and a repeat CBC in 48 hours timed after his shift.

Doctor: Welcome back. I see you are a 20-year-old male here for your follow-up on depression and medication. It has been six weeks since we started the sertraline. How have you been?
Patient: Better than before, but not great. I would say about halfway there.
Doctor: What is better and what is still bothering you?
Patient: I am getting out of bed on time most days and I went back to my classes. But I still feel down a lot of the time, I have low motivation, and I cannot concentrate when I study.
Doctor: How are your sleep and appetite?
Patient: Sleep is bad. I fall asleep fine with the trazodone, but I wake up at four and can't fall back asleep. Appetite is okay.
Doctor: Any side effects from the sertraline?
Patient: Some mild nausea in the first two weeks, but it is gone. No sexual problems, no headaches, and no sweating.
Doctor: Any thoughts of hurting yourself, or that life is not worth living?
Patient: No, nothing like that.
Doctor: Have there been periods when you felt unusually energetic, needed very little sleep, or had racing thoughts?
Patient: No, never.
Doctor: Any alcohol or drug use?
Patient: A few beers on weekends. No drugs.
Doctor: Remind me which medicines you take.
Patient: Sertraline 50 mg every morning and trazodone 50 mg at bedtime.
Doctor: And you are taking them regularly?
Patient: Yes, I have not missed any.
Doctor: Good. Your vitals today are blood pressure 118/72, heart rate 70, and weight 165 pounds, which is stable. Your PHQ-9 today is 14, down from 19 six weeks ago. Your TSH from intake was 2.0, which is normal. On exam you are calm and cooperative, your speech is normal, your mood is down, your affect is a little restricted, your thinking is organized, and you have no hallucinations and no suicidal thoughts.
Doctor: So you have major depressive disorder with a partial response, and you still have insomnia. I want to increase your sertraline from 50 to 100 mg every morning, and continue the trazodone 50 mg at bedtime. Keep going to your weekly therapy sessions and keep a regular sleep schedule. We will repeat the PHQ-9 in four weeks. Sometimes antidepressants can cause more anxiety or thoughts of self-harm in young adults when the dose changes, so call me or go to the emergency room if that happens.
Patient: Okay, that sounds good.

Sertraline was increased from 50 to 100 mg every morning, trazodone 50 mg at bedtime and weekly therapy continue, and the PHQ-9 will be repeated in four weeks.

Hospital day 2 for this 73-year-old female admitted with acute kidney injury from dehydration after four days of vomiting and watery diarrhea, presumed viral gastroenteritis. Her creatinine was 2.4 on admission, up from a baseline of 0.9. Overnight she had no fever and tolerated clear liquids. She has had two loose stools and no vomiting since admission. She denies abdominal pain, blood in the stool, dysuria, flank pain, and chest pain. She reports feeling less dizzy when she stands.

Her home lisinopril 20 mg daily for hypertension and hydrochlorothiazide 25 mg daily have been held since admission because of the kidney injury and volume depletion. She is receiving lactated Ringer's at 100 mL/h, potassium chloride 20 mEq by mouth twice today for low potassium, and ondansetron 4 mg IV as needed for nausea, of which she needed one dose overnight.

Vitals this morning are BP 108/62, up from 92/54 on admission, HR 88, RR 16, Temp 98.6 F, and SpO2 97% on room air. On exam her mucous membranes are slightly dry, JVP is flat, her heart is regular, her lungs are clear, her abdomen is soft and nontender, and she has no edema.

Labs this morning show creatinine 1.6, improved from 2.4, BUN 34, down from 52, potassium 3.5, up from 3.1, sodium 136, and bicarbonate 20. Urinalysis was bland with a specific gravity of 1.030 and no blood or protein, and FeNa was 0.6%, consistent with prerenal azotemia. Renal ultrasound showed no hydronephrosis.

Assessment is prerenal acute kidney injury from dehydration due to viral gastroenteritis, improving, with hypokalemia that is also improving. We will continue lactated Ringer's at 100 mL/h until she is drinking well, advance her diet as tolerated, and recheck creatinine and potassium this afternoon and tomorrow morning. note: Dictating a hospital day 2 progress note for an 82-year-old female admitted with community-acquired pneumonia. She was discharged from this hospital about three weeks ago after surgical repair of a wrist fracture, and she was admitted two days ago with cough, fever, and shortness of breath. This morning she says her cough is a little better and is still productive of yellow sputum. She denies chest pain, hemoptysis, nausea, and vomiting. Her only chronic condition is hypertension. Current antibiotics are ceftriaxone two grams, correction, one gram IV daily, and azithromycin 500 mg IV daily. Overnight her maximum temperature was 99.1. This morning blood pressure is 126/70, heart rate 84, respiratory rate 20, temperature 98.8, and oxygen saturation 94 percent on two liters nasal cannula. On exam she has crackles at the right base. There is no wheezing, no distress, the heart is regular, and there is no leg edema. The admission chest x-ray showed a right lower lobe infiltrate without effusion. White count this morning is 10.8, down from 13.2 on admission. Because of her recent hospitalization we checked a MRSA nasal PCR, which was negative, so no broader coverage is needed. Impression is community-acquired pneumonia, improving. Plan is to continue ceftriaxone and azithromycin, wean oxygen to room air with a goal saturation above 92 percent, incentive spirometry, and walking with physical therapy. Switch to oral antibiotics once she has been afebrile for 24 hours and is on room air. Anticipate discharge in one to two days with primary care follow up in one week and a repeat chest x-ray in six weeks.
